claims.text: A value object has no id, so nothing in it can serve as a row's key, and EF Core needs a key to track a row. So a value object that holds a single value, like Vnd, gets no table or key of its own: its value is stored in a column of its owner's row.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Keys; Keyless entity types (not tracked); Value Conversions; outline item 1

claims.text: PropertyBuilder.HasConversion(convertToProviderExpression, convertFromProviderExpression): the first expression is applied when EF Core writes the value to the database, the second when it reads the column value back into the property.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Configuring a value converter; HasConversion with two expressions)

claims.text: A property mapped with a value converter is stored in one column of the converter's provider type (int, PostgreSQL integer here) in the owning entity's table, and the model snapshot records it as Property<int> with HasColumnType("integer").
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (provider type); examples/don-hang @ stage-3 DonHangDbContextModelSnapshot.cs (OrderItem.UnitPrice)

claims.text: When EF Core loads an Order it uses Order's private parameterless constructor, so the public constructor's checks do not run (still true at stage-3).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3: DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs:69 (private Order()), :78 (public Order(...)); prereq design.l2.ef-core-and-private-setters

claims.text: If the read conversion throws (new Vnd(-1) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException), the exception propagates out of the query and the load fails; EF Core does not return the row with an unconverted value.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions; examples/don-hang @ stage-3 DonHang.Domain/Vnd.cs:12-16, DonHang.Tests/Domain/VndTests.cs:22-24

claims.text: At stage-3 db/schema.sql declares unit_price_vnd integer NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price_vnd > 0), so a table created from it refuses a negative unit price; the EF Core migrations add no such check.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3: db/schema.sql:30; DonHang.Infrastructure/Migrations/20260923154631_InitialCreate.cs (order_items, no check constraint)

claims.text: At stage-3 DonHangDbContext maps OrderItem to order_items with key (OrderId, ProductId) and maps UnitPrice to unit_price_vnd with HasConversion(price => price.Amount, amount => new Vnd(amount)); it has no Entity<Vnd> and no DbSet<Vnd>.

ASP.NET Core's default JSON options for controllers (web defaults) serialize the property UnitPriceVnd as "unitPriceVnd" (camelCase), so a client sees "unitPriceVnd": 450000 for a seed item priced 450000.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Format response data / System.Text.Json web defaults (JsonSerializerDefaults.Web, camelCase); examples/don-hang db/seed.sql (order 1, product 2)

claims.text: Keeping Vnd out of the DTO is worth it when clients already depend on the JSON shape: nesting the amount in an object would be a breaking change with no gain for them. Opposing context: a new API version with no existing clients may weigh a richer money shape.
claims.source_hint: outline item 5; prior lessons on breaking change and API versioning
